name: Proto-Danaw
notes: The parent of Maranao, Maguindanaon and Iranun, reconstructed by Allison (1979); Lobel (2013: 283) finds Allison's inventory (Table 9.1) accurate. Rows from Table 9.2 (p. 285), whose third column is headed 'PSPH/PGCPH'; they are stated here against Proto-Greater Central Philippine (decision lobel2013-danao). Proto-Danaw also had the homorganic clusters *bp, *dt, *ds, *gk, from PGCPH clusters of a voiced consonant and *p, *t, *s, *k (Table 9.2: '*Cp (if C = voiced)'); they survive in Iranun and Maguindanaon and give the Maranao heavy consonants (pp. 283-285). The assimilation of the first consonant is not entered as rows, because the table does not say which consonants it was. Glottocode dana1253 (Glottolog's Danaw: Maranao, Maguindanao, Iranun).
inherit_note: Table 9.2 pairs every Proto-Danaw phoneme with its PSPH/PGCPH source; what it shows unchanged is unchanged.

name: Maranao
notes: Phonology after Lobel (2013: ch. 9), which restates the analysis he published with Labi Riwarung in Oceanic Linguistics 48: 20 consonants and four vowels (Tables 9.3-9.4, p. 286). The four 'heavy' consonants, written p’ t’ k’ s’ by Lobel and ph, th, kh, z in Maranao spelling, come from the Proto-Danaw clusters *bp, *dt, *gk, *ds (Table 9.2); they 'are aspirated to varying degrees' and raise and tense the following vowel (pp. 276, 288-290). They do not occur in clusters or word-finally (p. 286). /h/ is found in three words, all Malay loans (p. 286). The glottal stop is phonemic only between vowels and word-finally (p. 286). No phonemic geminates; consonants are phonetically longer after schwa (p. 287). Not entered: schwa assimilation, epenthesis and syncope (§9.4.2-9.4.4) and the morphophonemics of §9.5. Coordinates from Glottolog 5.4.
inherit_note: Unchanged per Table 9.2 (p. 285), which gives the Proto-Danaw source of every Maranao phoneme.
